messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mateo, a 22-year-old product manager, was a civilian caught in the crossfire of an armed conflict in his home country two years ago. He was walking home from a market when a sudden volley of gunfire erupted from two directions, pinning him against a wall for what felt like an hour. Shots cracked from windows and alleyways; bodies fell nearby. He pressed himself flat, counting the shots, certain the next one would hit him. When the shooting finally stopped, he ran through the smoke, past shattered glass and blood, and did not stop until he reached his aunt’s apartment. That night, and for many nights after, he could not relax his shoulders or slow his heart.

Now living in a quiet American city, Mateo works as a product manager in a bright open-plan office. But his body has not left that alley. He feels constantly tense, as if bracing for impact—his jaw clenched, his stomach tight, his muscles coiled. Any unexpected movement nearby makes him flinch: a coworker stepping suddenly into his peripheral vision, a door swinging open too fast, a hand reaching across his desk. His heart lurches, and he scans the room for threats before he can remind himself he is safe. This hypervigilance is exhausting, but what exhausts him more is the way it drives him to do things he knows are not rational. When the tension becomes unbearable, Mateo finds himself checking his pulse over and over, pressing two fingers to his wrist, trying to convince himself that his heart rate is normal, that he is not about to die. He sometimes asks a colleague, “Do I look okay? My face—does it look pale?” The reassurance lasts only minutes before the vigilance starts again, because the very act of checking his body makes him more aware of every sensation—a twinge, a flutter, a tightness—which he then interprets as a sign of danger. He has also begun to hurt himself physically to release the overwhelming feelings: pressing his fingernails into his palms during meetings, or, in the privacy of his bathroom at night, scratching his forearm with the edge of a comb until the sting cuts through the fear.

The cycle tightens week by week. The more alert his body remains, the more urgently he reaches for these strategies to calm himself. But each strategy—reassurance seeking, body monitoring, self-harm—only sharpens his sense that something is wrong with him, that he must be in danger if he needs to check so frantically. He has started avoiding the subway because the sudden jolts and crowds trigger his startle response. At work, he sits with his back to the wall and watches the door, but he cannot avoid the sudden movements of others. Last week, when a coworker tapped his shoulder unexpectedly, Mateo spun around so violently that he knocked over his water bottle, then spent the next hour checking his pulse and asking three separate people if he looked pale. His manager noticed and asked if he was okay; Mateo lied and said he had not slept well.

What finally brought Mateo to therapy was an incident three days ago. In a meeting, a teammate stood up abruptly to gesture at a whiteboard. Mateo flinched so hard he scraped his thumb on the edge of his laptop, drawing blood. As he cleaned the cut in the restroom, he found himself pressing his thumbnail into the wound, deeper and deeper, until the pain felt like the only real thing in the room. He saw the look of alarm on his own face in the mirror, and for the first time he admitted he could not manage this alone. He is terrified that the cycle will never end—that his body will always be on alert, and that he will keep hurting himself just to feel something other than fear. But he is also, underneath that hope, afraid that he is broken beyond repair, that the alley he fled has followed him here and will never let go.
